section.title: The Temple Sermon
section.sectionRationale: Standing at the temple gate itself, Jeremiah confronts the nation's most cherished false security: the belief that God's presence in the building guarantees safety regardless of how they live. This sermon, delivered at the very seat of Judah's religious confidence, names the temple a den of robbers and warns that it can be destroyed exactly as Shiloh was, a warning Jesus Himself will later echo word for word.
section.thesis: Judah trusts in the temple's presence as a magical guarantee of safety while oppressing the vulnerable and worshipping other gods, but the LORD warns that a house that bears His Name is no substitute for obedience, and will be destroyed like Shiloh before it if the people do not truly amend their ways.
section.frameNote: Five movements: the call to amend ways and deeds rather than trust deceptive words; the warning of Shiloh's fate as precedent; the exposure of household idolatry to the Queen of Heaven; the declaration that obedience, not sacrifice, was always the true command; and the vision of Topheth turned into the Valley of Slaughter.

units.label: Amend your ways
units.note: do not trust in deceptive words: this is the temple of the LORD

verses.text: This is the word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD, saying,
“Stand in the gate of the house of the LORD and proclaim this message: Hear the word of the LORD, all you people of Judah who enter through these gates to worship the LORD.
Thus says the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel: Correct your ways and deeds, and I will let you live in this place.

Do not trust in deceptive words, chanting: 
‘This is the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD, 
the temple of the LORD.’
For if you really correct your ways and deeds, if you act justly toward one another,
if you no longer oppress the foreigner and the fatherless and the widow, and if you no longer shed innocent blood in this place or follow other gods to your own harm,
then I will let you live in this place, in the land that I gave to your fathers forever and ever.
But look, you keep trusting in deceptive words to no avail.
Will you steal and murder, commit adultery and perjury, burn incense to Baal, and follow other gods that you have not known,
and then come and stand before Me in this house, which bears My Name, and say, ‘We are delivered, so we can continue with all these abominations’?
Has this house, which bears My Name, become a {{beit_peritsim|den of robbers}} in your sight? Yes, I too have seen it, declares the LORD.

units.label: Remember Shiloh
units.note: what I did there, I will do here

verses.text: But go now to the place in Shiloh where I first made a dwelling for My Name, and see what I did to it because of the wickedness of My people Israel.
And now, because you have done all these things, declares the LORD, and because I have spoken to you again and again but you would not listen, and I have called to you but you would not answer,
therefore what I did to Shiloh I will now do to the house that bears My Name, the house in which you trust, the place that I gave to you and your fathers.
And I will cast you out of My presence, just as I have cast out all your brothers, all the descendants of Ephraim.

units.label: The Queen of Heaven
units.note: do not pray for this people

verses.text: As for you, do not pray for these people, do not offer a plea or petition on their behalf, and do not beg Me, for I will not listen to you.
Do you not see what they are doing in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem?
The sons gather wood, the fathers light the fire, and the women knead the dough to make cakes for the Queen of Heaven; they pour out drink offerings to other gods to provoke Me to anger.
But am I the One they are provoking? declares the LORD. Is it not themselves they spite, to their own shame?

Therefore this is what the Lord GOD says: Behold, My anger and My fury will be poured out on this place, on man and beast, on the trees of the field and the produce of the land, and it will burn and not be extinguished.

units.label: Obedience, not sacrifice
units.note: the command was always to listen

verses.text: This is what the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel, says: Add your burnt offerings to your other sacrifices and eat the meat yourselves!
For when I brought your fathers out of the land of Egypt, I did not merely command them about burnt offerings and sacrifices,
but this is what I commanded them: {{shama|Obey}} Me, and I will be your God, and you will be My people. You must walk in all the ways I have commanded you, so that it may go well with you.
Yet they did not listen or incline their ear, but they followed the stubborn inclinations of their own evil hearts. They went backward and not forward.
From the day your fathers came out of the land of Egypt until this day, I have sent you all My servants the prophets again and again.
Yet they would not listen to Me or incline their ear, but they stiffened their necks and did more evil than their fathers.
When you tell them all these things, they will not listen to you. When you call to them, they will not answer.
Therefore you must say to them, ‘This is the nation that would not listen to the voice of the LORD their God and would not receive correction. Truth has perished; it has disappeared from their lips.’

units.label: Topheth: the Valley of Slaughter
units.note: children in the fire, an evil never commanded

verses.text: Cut off your hair and throw it away. Raise up a lamentation on the barren heights, for the LORD has rejected and forsaken the generation of His wrath.’
For the people of Judah have done evil in My sight, declares the LORD. They have set up their abominations in the house that bears My Name, and so have defiled it.
They have built the high places of {{gehinnom|Topheth}} in the Valley of Hinnom so they could burn their sons and daughters in the fire, something I never commanded, nor did it even enter My mind.

So behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when this place will no longer be called Topheth and the Valley of Hinnom, but the Valley of Slaughter. For they will bury the dead in Topheth until there is no more room.
The corpses of this people will become food for the birds of the air and the beasts of the earth, and there will be no one to scare them away.
I will remove from the cities of Judah and the streets of Jerusalem the sounds of joy and gladness and the voices of the bride and bridegroom, for the land will become a wasteland.”

“At that time,” declares the LORD, “the bones of the kings of Judah, the bones of the officials, the bones of the priests, the bones of the prophets, and the bones of the people of Jerusalem will be removed from their graves.

They will be exposed to the sun and moon, and to all the host of heaven which they have loved, served, followed, consulted, and worshiped. Their bones will not be gathered up or buried, but will become like dung lying on the ground.
And wherever I have banished them, the remnant of this evil family will choose death over life,” declares the LORD of Hosts.

beit_peritsim.gloss: Den of robbers, literally house of violent men. The charge is not that crimes happened in the temple itself but that the temple had become a hideout, a place people ran to for false security after committing crimes elsewhere, exactly the phrase Jesus quotes when He cleanses the temple, Mark 11:17.

shama.gloss: To hear, listen, and by extension obey; in Hebrew there is no separate word for obedience apart from truly hearing. God's original command at the exodus was fundamentally this, listen to My voice, making ritual sacrifice always secondary to a heart that actually hears and responds.

gehinnom.gloss: The Valley of Hinnom, site of the horrific child sacrifices to Molech at Topheth. This valley's name became, by the New Testament era, the Greek Gehenna, Jesus' most common word for final judgment and hell, a direct line from this literal valley of atrocity to the ultimate reality it came to symbolize.

basic.context: Jeremiah stands at the temple gate itself and confronts the crowd's favorite chant, this is the temple of the LORD, as a dangerous lie. God's presence in the building was never a magic guarantee of safety; it always required lives that matched the worship, justice for the vulnerable and loyalty to God alone. Jeremiah warns that the very temple they trust can be destroyed exactly as Shiloh, the earlier dwelling place of God's Name, already was.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a real sermon delivered at a real location, the temple gate, confronting Judah's specific presumption that the temple's presence guaranteed unconditional protection. The hardest truth to hear plainly is that religious buildings, rituals, and even correct theological language, this is the temple of the LORD, provide no automatic safety when the life behind them is corrupt; God's own house can become, in His own words, a den of robbers and be destroyed.
basic.originalLanguages: Judah has turned God's house into a beit peritsim, a den of robbers, not where crimes happen but where criminals flee for false safety after committing them elsewhere. God's foundational command was always to shama, hear and obey, one Hebrew word doing both jobs, showing that true worship was never separable from a listening, responsive life. The horrors at gehinnom, the Valley of Hinnom, later gave its name to Gehenna, Jesus' own word for final judgment.
basic.typology: The temple sermon's warning that God's own house can be destroyed for hollow religion anticipates Jesus' cleansing of the temple, where He quotes this exact den of robbers language, Mark 11:17, and it anticipates the temple's actual destruction in AD 70. The Valley of Hinnom's horrors become, by Jesus' day, the very name and image He uses for final judgment, Gehenna.
basic.christ: Jesus deliberately quotes Jeremiah 7:11 word for word when He cleanses the temple, has this house not become a den of robbers, Mark 11:17, standing in the line of this very sermon and applying it directly to the temple of His own generation. Jesus also repeatedly warns of Gehenna, the very valley named in this passage, showing that the judgment Jeremiah announced here for hollow religion becomes, in Christ's teaching, the abiding warning about final judgment for every generation.
basic.god: God is patient, having sent prophets again and again before this final warning, yet He will not be manipulated by correct religious language detached from a changed life; His own Name dwelling in a place never obligates Him to protect that place regardless of the wickedness inside it. His justice is severe enough to destroy His own house, yet He states plainly that even the horror of child sacrifice at Topheth was never something He commanded or even conceived.
basic.crossReferences: Mark 11:15-17 has Jesus quote Jeremiah 7:11 directly when cleansing the temple. 1 Samuel 4:1-11 records the actual, historical loss of the ark and the fall of Shiloh referenced as precedent. Matthew 5:22 and 10:28 have Jesus use Gehenna, drawn from this very valley, as His term for final judgment. 1 Samuel 15:22 states the same priority, to obey is better than sacrifice, that this sermon insists on.
basic.oneStory: This is the exposure of hollow religion at its most dangerous, trust in a building, a chant, or a ritual as a substitute for a changed life. Jesus stands in direct continuity with this warning, quoting it as He cleanses the temple of His own day and turning the very valley named here into His enduring image of final judgment, calling every generation to the obedience Jeremiah's audience refused.

context.literary:
This is one of the few long prose sermons in the book, and it is built with a careful eye for repetition. Four phrases carry the structure. The first is the chant of verse 4, 'the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD,' three times, which is the sound of a people reassuring themselves. The second is 'deceptive words,' verses 4 and 8, which brackets the first section. The third is the Hebrew idiom for ownership, 'the house that bears My Name,' which occurs in verses 10, 11, 14 and 30. The fourth is 'this place,' which appears in verses 3, 6, 7, 14, 20 and 32, so that the sermon keeps circling the one location the people thought safe.

The movement runs in four steps. Verses 1 to 15 are the gate sermon proper: a condition, a slogan, a list of crimes, and a case from history. Verses 16 to 20 abruptly turn to Jeremiah and forbid him to pray, then show the family at work on cakes for the Queen of Heaven. Verses 21 to 28 take up the sacrifices and the question of what God ever required. Verses 29 to 34 and 8:1 to 3 become a funeral song for the valley and for the dead.

The list of crimes in verse 9 follows the order of the commandments, theft, murder, adultery, false oaths, and then idols, in the same way Hosea 4:2 does. It is a summary of the Decalogue set at the door of the temple. Verses 5 to 7 give the one positive condition in the chapter, 'if you really correct your ways,' and the one gracious promise, 'I will let you live in this place.' The sermon's tragedy is that the condition goes unmet.

The ending is a macabre reversal. The people who loved, served, followed, consulted and worshiped the sun, moon and stars will have their bones dug up and spread under them, 8:1 and 2. The last line of the unit, 'choose death over life,' 8:3, turns Deuteronomy 30:19 on its head.
context.historical:
Jeremiah 26:1 places a temple sermon at the beginning of Jehoiakim's reign, around 609 BC, shortly after Josiah's death, and most readers take chapters 7 and 26 as two accounts of the same event, one giving the content and the other the aftermath. In 26:7 to 9 the priests, prophets and people seize him and shout, 'You must surely die!' Elders then recall that Micah had once said Zion would be plowed like a field, Micah 3:12, and Hezekiah had not killed him. A later prophet, Uriah, did not fare so well. Jehoiakim had him brought back from Egypt and put to the sword, Jeremiah 26:20-23. Preaching in the temple court was dangerous.

The belief Jeremiah attacks had deep roots. The psalms of Zion proclaimed, 'God is within her; she will not be moved,' Psalm 46:5, and when Sennacherib's army was struck down outside the city in 701, the story became a proof that Jerusalem would never fall, 2 Kings 19:35. Solomon's prayer asked God to keep His eyes open toward the temple, 1 Kings 8:29, and the people heard that as a guarantee. They overlooked the condition in 1 Kings 9:6-9 that if Israel turned away, God would cast out of His sight 'this temple I have sanctified for My Name.'

Shiloh was the earlier home of the tabernacle, where Israel assembled and set up the Tent of Meeting, Joshua 18:1. When the ark was captured by the Philistines in Eli's day, 1 Samuel 4:11, Shiloh's place was lost. Psalm 78:60 says that God 'abandoned the tabernacle of Shiloh.' The Bible does not describe Shiloh's destruction in detail, but Jeremiah uses it as a well known warning.

The Queen of Heaven is generally taken to be a Mesopotamian love and war goddess, Ishtar or her Canaanite counterpart, and the picture of entire families baking cakes is confirmed by Jeremiah 44:17-19, where the women defend the practice. Topheth lay in the Valley of Hinnom, south and west of the city, where children were burned, a practice Leviticus 18:21 forbids and 2 Kings 21:6 attributes to Manasseh. Josiah had defiled the site, 2 Kings 23:10, which shows how quickly the cult returned.
context.canonical:
The sermon belongs to a larger conversation in Scripture about what a sanctuary is for. Solomon, at its dedication, admitted, 'But will God indeed dwell upon the earth? Even heaven, the highest heaven, cannot contain You, much less this temple I have built,' 1 Kings 8:27. Isaiah heard God ask, 'What kind of house will you build for Me?' and say that He esteems 'he who is humble and contrite in spirit, who trembles at My word,' Isaiah 66:1-2. Stephen quotes that passage against those who treated the temple as God's residence, Acts 7:48.

The preference for obedience over sacrifice runs through the prophets. 'Obedience is better than sacrifice,' 1 Samuel 15:22. 'I desire mercy, not sacrifice,' Hosea 6:6, which Jesus twice quotes, Matthew 9:13 and 12:7. Isaiah 1:11-17 and Amos 5:21-24 say the LORD hates festivals attended by guilty people, and Micah 6:6-8 asks the question outright and answers it with justice, mercy and humble walking. Jeremiah 7 is the sharpest of these because it is preached at the door of the temple itself.

The aftermath is told elsewhere. Ezekiel sees the glory of the LORD leave the temple in two stages, Ezekiel 10:18-19 and 11:22-23. Lamentations speaks of the Lord who 'has rejected His altar; He has abandoned His sanctuary,' Lamentations 2:7. Jeremiah 7:11 is then quoted at the climax of Jesus' ministry in Jerusalem: 'But you have made it a den of robbers,' Mark 11:17, with Matthew 21:13 and Luke 19:46. Jesus also predicts that not one stone will be left on another, Mark 13:2, and says of Himself that He will raise the temple of His body, John 2:19-21.

The valley of Hinnom closes the thread. Jesus' warnings about 'hell' in Matthew 5:22 and 10:28 and Mark 9:43-48 use the Greek form of its name, Gehenna, and Mark's 'their worm never dies, and the fire is never quenched' quotes Isaiah 66:24. The temple of stone gives way to the temple of people, 1 Corinthians 3:16, and finally to a city with no temple, because 'the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple,' Revelation 21:22.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The sermon intends to unseat a creed. 'This is the temple of the LORD' was a true statement used as a false promise, and Jeremiah wants the crowd to hear their own chant as a charm. The speech is not an attack on the temple or on worship. It is an attack on using worship as insurance, going from the house of God to the next round of theft and adultery and then returning for a clean slate, verses 9 and 10.

It also intends to leave the door open. Twice the LORD says the words, 'I will let you live in this place,' verses 3 and 7, on the condition that ways and deeds are corrected. The hearers are given a real choice, and the chapter would have no tension if the outcome were already settled. Jeremiah 26:3 says as much: 'Perhaps they will listen and turn.'

For the readers who came later, in exile, it explains what had happened. The destruction of the house was not a defeat of God by Babylon's gods. The LORD had said, in advance and at the gate, that He would do to the temple what He had done to Shiloh, verse 14. The book's exiles could see that He had warned them, and that the message they were meant to carry out of the ruins was that God's presence is a gift to be honoured, not a possession.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Several things in this sermon are descriptions or addressed instructions rather than rules for everyone. The prohibition on prayer in verse 16, 'do not pray for these people,' was addressed to Jeremiah at a specific moment and is repeated to him in 11:14 and 14:11. It is not a rule that the church should stop praying for the lost, and Jesus taught the opposite, 'love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you,' Matthew 5:44. The ironic order in verse 21, 'Add your burnt offerings to your other sacrifices and eat the meat yourselves,' is sarcasm, not instruction.

The description of the Queen of Heaven's cult and the child burning at Topheth records what Judah did, not anything to imitate and not anything God ever commanded. The text takes care to say so about Topheth: 'something I never commanded, nor did it even enter My mind,' verse 31.

The prescriptive elements are the moral ones. Correct your ways, act justly, do not oppress the foreigner, the fatherless and the widow, do not shed innocent blood, do not follow other gods, verses 5 and 6. These are stated as binding on those who claim to worship the LORD. The warning is also for us: a church building, a creed, a liturgy or a family reputation is not a guarantee. The New Testament uses the same logic when it says believers are God's temple and warns that God will destroy those who destroy it, 1 Corinthians 3:16-17.

debates.question: Does verse 22 say God never commanded sacrifices?

views.label: A forceful way of saying obedience comes first
views.case: The Hebrew of verse 22 literally says that God did not speak with their fathers or command them 'concerning matters of burnt offering and sacrifice.' Yet Leviticus gave extensive rules for sacrifice. Many read the sentence as a Hebrew way of setting two things side by side, where 'not this but that' means 'not this so much as that.' The BSB's 'did not merely command' takes this view. Hosea 6:6 and 1 Samuel 15:22 use the same logic.

views.label: A claim about what was foundational at the exodus
views.case: Others take the text more literally. At the exodus, the first covenant words were 'Obey Me, and I will be your God,' as verse 23 quotes, and the detailed sacrificial system was given later and for the purpose of dealing with sin. On this reading Jeremiah is saying the heart of the covenant never was the altar.

views.label: A direct attack on the sacrificial system
views.case: A smaller group reads the verse as denying that sacrifice was ever commanded. This is hard to square with the laws of Leviticus and with Jeremiah's own later promises that priests and offerings would again be part of the restored people, Jeremiah 33:18.

debates.bearing: The first two views agree about the point: God was never after ritual as a replacement for a changed life. Hebrews 10:5-9 uses the same prophetic logic to say that sacrifices were never the final answer, and that the obedient 'I have come to do Your will' is what God desired.

debates.question: Are chapters 7 and 26 two versions of the same sermon?

views.label: The same event
views.case: Both place Jeremiah in the temple, both speak of making the house like Shiloh, and both draw a hostile response. Chapter 26 dates it to the beginning of Jehoiakim's reign, Jeremiah 26:1. On this view chapter 7 gives the extended sermon and chapter 26 the narrative of the trial that followed, with some phrases abbreviated.

views.label: Two separate occasions
views.case: Chapter 7 has no date, includes material not present in chapter 26, such as the Queen of Heaven and Topheth, and Jeremiah's message could have been repeated more than once. Topheth was defiled by Josiah, 2 Kings 23:10, so a sermon in the later years of that king might not mention it as an active practice, which suggests a different time.

debates.bearing: The main teaching is unaffected. The point of both chapters is the same: the temple's presence is no guarantee. Seeing chapter 26 as the response gives the sermon its human cost, since Jeremiah is nearly killed, which helps readers feel the weight of what he was saying.

debates.question: Why is Jeremiah forbidden to pray for the people?

views.label: A judicial closing of the door for that generation
views.case: The ban is repeated, Jeremiah 7:16, 11:14, 14:11, and 15:1 adds that even Moses and Samuel could not turn God's heart. On this view the time for intercession is past, in the same way that 1 John 5:16 speaks of a sin not to be prayed about.

views.label: A shock to remove false confidence
views.case: Others read the ban as a rhetorical way to drive home how serious things have become. Jeremiah does continue to speak, and later tells the exiles to pray for Babylon's welfare, Jeremiah 29:7, and the same God promises to listen again when they call, Jeremiah 29:12.

debates.bearing: Whichever view is taken, the ban is a measure of seriousness and not a general rule. Believers are told to pray for their enemies, and Christ 'is interceding for us,' Romans 8:34.

study.originalLanguages:
The first demand in verse 3 is 'Correct your ways and deeds.' The verb is heitiv, from yatav, to be good, so the sense is 'make your ways good.' In verse 5 the demand is strengthened by the Hebrew device of repeating the verb, 'if you really correct,' which is the force of an infinitive set beside the finite verb. It is a call for real repair, not a ritual adjustment.

The promise attached is 'I will let you live in this place.' The verb is shakan, to dwell, in a form that means 'I will cause you to dwell.' It is the root behind mishkan, the tabernacle, and the idea of God's own dwelling. In verse 12 the LORD says Shiloh was the place where He 'first made a dwelling for My Name,' from the same verb. The two uses sit together on purpose. God dwells with people who walk with Him, and people dwell where He dwells. When His presence is treated as a charm, both kinds of dwelling are at risk.

The phrase 'the house which bears My Name' repeated in verses 10, 11, 14 and 30 is literally 'the house over which My Name has been called.' It is the formula of ownership. To call a name over something is to claim it. The temple is God's, and that is exactly why it will not protect those who misuse it.

In verse 11 the BSB gives 'den of robbers.' The Hebrew is me'arat peritsim, 'a cave of violent men,' and the word peritsim comes from parats, to break through or burst out. These are people who break in. The point is not that robbery is committed in the temple but that it has become the burrow to which robbers retreat. The Greek Old Testament renders it with the same words that Jesus uses in the Gospels, which is why His citation is so exact.

The warning of verse 31 that child burning was 'something I never commanded, nor did it even enter My mind' is, literally, that it 'did not come up upon My heart.' It is the most intimate language of denial in the book. Topheth's meaning is uncertain, but the Valley of Ben Hinnom, ge hinnom, is the origin of the Greek Gehenna.

Finally, in 8:2 the people 'loved, served, followed, consulted and worshiped' the host of heaven. The fourth verb is darash, to seek, the same verb used for seeking God in Deuteronomy 4:29 and Amos 5:4. The people did seek, but they sought the wrong lights. And in 8:3 the remnant will 'choose death over life,' an echo of the choice in Deuteronomy 30:19, which Moses set before them with the words 'Therefore choose life.'

typology.type: The temple called a den of robbers, Jeremiah 7:11
typology.fulfillment: Jesus enters the temple courts, overturns the tables and says, 'It is written: My house will be a house of prayer. But you have made it a den of robbers,' Luke 19:46. He combines Isaiah 56:7 and Jeremiah 7:11, the promise and the indictment, in one sentence. The correspondence is that He acts as Jeremiah did at the same place, with the same charge: religion used as cover. The escalation is that Jeremiah spoke at the gate and was seized, while Jesus drives out the sellers and then heals in the temple, Matthew 21:14. The type falls short because the cleansing did not prevent the destruction that He then foretold, Mark 13:2.

typology.type: Shiloh's fate for the house that bears the Name, Jeremiah 7:12-14
typology.fulfillment: The warning that the LORD will do to this temple what He did to Shiloh is repeated in Jesus' words, 'not one stone here will be left on another,' Matthew 24:2. The correspondence is that a sanctuary can be left empty when its people reject God's word. The deeper fulfilment lies in the claim that Jesus Himself is the true temple, 'Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up again,' John 2:19-21. The charge brought against Him, Matthew 26:61, echoes the charge brought against Jeremiah. The type is limited because the old temple was a shadow, and its loss was not the loss of God's presence but the preparing of a better one, Ephesians 2:21-22.

typology.type: Topheth and the Valley of Hinnom, Jeremiah 7:31-32
typology.fulfillment: A place of burning children, renamed the Valley of Slaughter, becomes the Greek Gehenna on Jesus' lips. He warns, 'fear the One who can destroy both soul and body in hell,' Matthew 10:28, and speaks of the place where 'their worm never dies, and the fire is never quenched,' Mark 9:48, quoting Isaiah 66:24. The correspondence is that a real place of judgment on earth becomes the picture of final judgment. The text does not describe Gehenna as an eternal state itself, so the link is the use of the name as an image. The type falls short because the valley was a place of human cruelty, and the final judgment is the act of a God who never commanded such things.

God's first word at the exodus was 'Obey Me, and I will be your God.' Hebrews 10:5-9 shows Christ stepping into history and saying, 'Sacrifice and offering You did not desire, but a body You prepared for Me... I have come to do Your will, O God.' He is the first person to give God the obedience Judah did not. The escalation is that His obedience is also the sacrifice, so the two things Jeremiah's hearers set against each other are held together. The type has limits, since Jeremiah's hearers were called to obey while Christ's obedience is also given for those who failed.

typology.type: The prophet on trial for his words about the temple, Jeremiah 26:8-9
typology.fulfillment: Jeremiah was seized and told, 'You must surely die!' for saying the house would become like Shiloh. Jesus is accused of saying He would destroy the temple, Mark 14:58, and Stephen is charged with the same, Acts 6:13-14. The correspondence is the pattern of a true word against a sacred institution being treated as blasphemy. The escalation is that Jeremiah was delivered by the elders' memory of Micah, while Jesus was condemned. The pattern is incomplete because Jeremiah was a witness to judgment, while Jesus is both the witness and the one who bears it.

study.christ:
The strongest link is the direct quotation. When Jesus drives the traders from the temple court He says, 'But you have made it a den of robbers,' Luke 19:46, and the words are Jeremiah's, spoken from the same steps. The Gospels record His act as a deliberate return to this sermon. Jeremiah stood at the gate and said that the house which bears God's Name is not a hiding place for the guilty. Jesus enters the house and acts on the same words. John adds that the disciples remembered the verse, 'Zeal for Your house will consume Me,' John 2:17. He is not an outsider attacking the temple but the one who loves it enough to cleanse it, and who, like Jeremiah, will be accused of threatening it.

The sermon also leads to Christ by its ownership language. The house 'bears My Name,' and in John 1:14 the Word 'made His dwelling among us,' the verb of the tabernacle. Jesus says in John 2:19 that the temple He will raise is His body. The question the sermon raises, where can God be met safely, is answered by the person in whom God's presence has come as man. The temple was always a promise as well as a place, and Jeremiah 7 shows the promise being abused. In Jesus the promise is kept. Paul takes the same step with the church, 'built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus Himself as the cornerstone,' Ephesians 2:20-22, and Peter calls believers living stones, 1 Peter 2:5.

The call to obedience also leads to Christ. In verse 23 God's first word was 'Obey Me.' The only one who ever gave a life of complete obedience is Jesus, who said in the words of the psalm, 'I have come to do Your will, O God,' Hebrews 10:7. The sacrifices Jeremiah declared empty without obedience are completed in One whose obedience and sacrifice are the same act. Paul sets His obedience against Adam's disobedience, Romans 5:19. Because of this, those who cannot obey are not left to the verdict of verse 28, 'Truth has perished,' but are given the obedience of another and the Spirit to begin walking in it.

Finally, Jeremiah's own position points ahead. He is forbidden to pray, rejected by the leaders, and nearly killed, and he continues to speak. Jesus, hated and condemned in the same city for similar words, prays 'Father, forgive them,' Luke 23:34, where Jeremiah was told not to. Hebrews says that He 'always lives to intercede,' Hebrews 7:25. The prohibition on prayer was true for that generation, but the Son's intercession cannot be shut out.

A caution applies. Jeremiah 7 does not secretly describe Jesus' ministry. It is a warning about hollow religion, and the New Testament recognises Jesus as the one who both applies the warning and removes its cause.
study.god:
The God of this sermon is first of all a God who speaks again and again. 'I have spoken to you again and again but you would not listen, and I have called to you but you would not answer,' verse 13, and the footnote notes that the Hebrew says He spoke 'rising up early,' the image of a household head who gets up before dawn to send a message. Verse 25 uses the same idiom of the prophets: He sent them 'rising up early and sending.' The Chronicler gives the explanation, that the LORD did this 'because He had compassion on them and on His dwelling place,' 2 Chronicles 36:15. The patience in the chapter is long, and the anger is the end of that patience, not the first resort.

He is a God who cannot be possessed. Verse 4 shows a people who think they can hold Him by repeating His address. The LORD insists that His Name on the house does not oblige Him to defend it against His own word, verse 14. This is not coldness. It is the freedom of the God who made heaven and earth and whom heaven cannot contain, 1 Kings 8:27. He gave the house, and He can take it back without ceasing to be God. The loss of the house does not mean the loss of God, as Ezekiel will show when the glory goes with the exiles.

He is a God who cares more about justice than ceremonies. Verses 5 and 6 name the foreigner, the fatherless and the widow before they name the gods. The charge in verse 9 is the moral law, and the offences are committed against neighbours. This matches God's own character in Exodus 34:6-7, compassionate and gracious and yet not leaving the guilty unpunished. Worship that does not touch the fatherless is worship of someone else.

He is a God who is wounded by sin and also unwilling to be made its author. Verse 19 asks 'Is it Me they are provoking? Is it not themselves they spite?' which shows that God's anger is a response to people harming themselves as well as Him. Verse 31 says the burning of children never entered His mind. He is not responsible for human cruelty, and He is not indifferent to it. For anyone troubled by harsh judgments in Scripture, this verse sets a limit: the evil is the people's, and the judgment is a response.

He is a God who holds out a real condition and a real consequence at the same time. 'Then I will let you live in this place,' verse 7, is a promise that is open until the end. And He is holy enough to bring about the end of the house when the condition is refused.

For worship, the sermon is a reminder to examine what we say at the door. The question is not whether we sing and pray but whether the God we come to meet has any say in how we live afterward. He does, and He is still the God who says, 'Obey Me, and I will be your God, and you will be My people,' verse 23.

crossReferences.note: Jesus overturns the tables and quotes Jeremiah 7:11 with Isaiah 56:7. The Gospel record makes the sermon's charge His own, and shows He saw the temple of His day in the same condition as the one at the gate of Jeremiah's.

The narrative of what happened when Jeremiah spoke these words. The priests, prophets and people seize him and demand his death for saying the house will become like Shiloh. It shows how dear the false confidence was.
Israel treated the ark as a charm against the Philistines and lost the battle and the ark. Jeremiah's use of Shiloh recalls an earlier case of trusting a sacred object instead of the God who gave it.

The psalm says God abandoned the tabernacle of Shiloh and delivered His strength to captivity. It gives the historical memory behind verse 12, and shows that the loss of a sanctuary was part of Israel's own songs.

God told Solomon that if Israel turned away He would banish from His presence the temple He had sanctified, and it would become a heap of rubble. Jeremiah is not inventing a threat. He is repeating the terms on which the temple was given.

'I desire mercy, not sacrifice, and the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings.' It gives the same priority as Jeremiah 7:21-23. Jesus quotes it twice in Matthew, to defend mercy against those who valued ritual correctness.

Samuel tells Saul that obedience is better than sacrifice, and attentiveness better than the fat of rams. The principle is as old as the monarchy, which shows Jeremiah was not introducing a new principle but recalling Israel's own history.

Jesus tells His hearers to fear the One who can destroy both soul and body in hell, using the Greek name for the Valley of Hinnom. The valley of Jeremiah 7:31-32 is the origin of the New Testament's word for final judgment.

God asks what house they could build for One whose throne is heaven, and says He esteems the humble and contrite person who trembles at His word. It is the principle behind the temple sermon in its most compact form.

Years later the women of Judah defend their worship of the Queen of Heaven, saying they had plenty when they served her. It confirms how deep the practice of Jeremiah 7:18 went, and how little it was ended by disaster.

The glory of the LORD leaves the threshold of the temple and rises above the cherubim. It shows what the loss of the house meant in practice: God's presence moves out before the building is destroyed.

Jesus says 'Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up again,' speaking of the temple of His body. The place where God is met safely is a person, and the sermon's question about the temple is answered in Him.

study.oneStory:
The question behind this sermon begins in Eden. In the garden God walked with His people, and the loss of that walking is the loss of everything. From then on the Bible follows God's moves to come near again: the tent in the wilderness, the tabernacle at Shiloh, the temple in Jerusalem. Each is a gift of presence, and each is also given on terms. 'Obey Me, and I will be your God,' verse 23, is the covenant formula, and the buildings are meant to serve that relationship, not replace it.

Jeremiah 7 is the chapter in which this long line of dwelling places runs into the same wall as the garden. Adam could not stay in the garden by possessing it; Israel could not stay in the land and in the temple by repeating the chant. The sermon's 'then I will let you live in this place' is Eden's question again: will you live in My presence on My terms? Verse 14's 'what I did to Shiloh I will now do' is the second exile from a sanctuary, and the bones of chapter 8 show that the first consequence of lost presence is death.

The story does not end with the loss. Jeremiah himself goes on to promise a new covenant with God's law written on the heart, Jeremiah 31:33, and a future in which people will no longer speak of the ark of the covenant, because the whole city will be called the throne of the LORD, Jeremiah 3:16-17. The prophets look ahead to a presence that does not depend on a building. Ezekiel sees the glory depart and then return, and a river flow from a new temple.

The Gospels carry the story forward at the same address. Jesus enters the temple, repeats Jeremiah's words, predicts the loss of the stones, and speaks of His own body as the place of meeting, John 2:19-21. After His resurrection the Spirit makes the church the temple, 1 Corinthians 3:16, and believers are built together into a dwelling place for God, Ephesians 2:22. The obedience Judah would not give is given by Christ, and the death of sacrifice is replaced by the sacrifice He made of Himself, Hebrews 10:9-10.

The story arrives at the new creation, where John says, 'I saw no temple in the city, because the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple,' Revelation 21:22. The slogan Jeremiah's hearers chanted is finally true, but not as they meant it. The temple of the LORD is no longer a building to be trusted. It is the presence of God Himself among His people, with no more death or mourning or crying or pain, Revelation 21:4, and nothing impure enters it, 21:27. The people who once had to be warned at the gate walk through its gates unafraid.

sermon.title: In the Temple
sermon.why: Begg reads Jeremiah 7:1-11 alongside Mark 11:15-19, showing that Jesus' cleansing of the temple deliberately quotes and enacts this very temple sermon, exactly the connection this study draws between Jeremiah's warning and Christ's own confrontation with hollow religion.

quiz.q: What false confidence does Jeremiah confront the people with at the temple gate?

options.text: That chanting 'this is the temple of the LORD' guarantees safety regardless of how they live.
options.note: Verse 4 names this exact chant as deceptive words the people wrongly trusted.

options.text: That the temple had already been destroyed and could not be rebuilt.
options.note: The temple is still standing at this point; the false confidence is trust in its presence, not concern over its destruction.

options.text: That sacrifices were no longer being offered at all.
options.note: Sacrifices were still being offered, verse 21, but as a substitute for obedience rather than an expression of it.

options.text: That foreign nations had already been defeated permanently.
options.note: The passage is about religious presumption tied to the temple building, not military claims about foreign nations.

quiz.q: What historical precedent does God cite to warn that the temple is not automatically safe?

options.text: Shiloh, the earlier dwelling place of God's Name, which He destroyed for Israel's wickedness.
options.note: Verses 12-14 explicitly cite Shiloh's destruction as the pattern that could repeat at Jerusalem's temple.

options.text: The building of Solomon's original temple.
options.note: The temple's construction is not the precedent cited; its destruction, foreshadowed by Shiloh, is the warning.

options.text: The exodus from Egypt under Moses.
options.note: The exodus is referenced later regarding obedience, verse 22, but Shiloh is the specific precedent for the temple's possible destruction.

options.text: The reign of King David.
options.note: David's reign is not the precedent cited here; Shiloh's destruction under the judges is the specific warning example.

quiz.q: According to verses 22-23, what did God command Israel's fathers most fundamentally at the exodus?

options.text: To obey His voice, so that He would be their God and they His people.
options.note: Verse 23 states this was the foundational command, prior to and more basic than the sacrificial system.

options.text: To build the tabernacle before anything else.
options.note: The tabernacle's construction followed the giving of the law, but the fundamental command cited here is to obey God's voice.

options.text: To offer burnt offerings as the primary requirement.
options.note: The text explicitly says this was not merely a command about sacrifices; obedience was the deeper requirement.

options.text: To conquer Canaan immediately upon leaving Egypt.
options.note: Conquest is not the subject of this verse; the command cited concerns obedience to God's voice.

quiz.q: What horrific practice at Topheth does God say He never commanded?

options.text: Burning their sons and daughters in the fire as child sacrifice.
options.note: Verse 31 states plainly this was never commanded and never even entered God's mind.

options.text: Offering grain and incense at the temple.
options.note: These were legitimate, commanded elements of worship; the horror described is child sacrifice, not grain offerings.

options.text: Fasting during times of national mourning.
options.note: Fasting is not the practice condemned in this passage; child sacrifice at Topheth is.

options.text: Celebrating annual harvest festivals.
options.note: Harvest festivals were legitimately commanded elsewhere; this passage condemns the specific atrocity of child sacrifice.

quiz.q: How does Jesus later connect Himself directly to this sermon?

options.text: He quotes Jeremiah 7:11 word for word while cleansing the temple of His own day.
options.note: Mark 11:17 records Jesus using the exact den of robbers language from this passage during the temple cleansing.

options.text: He has no recorded connection to this sermon anywhere in the Gospels.
options.note: Jesus explicitly quotes this passage in Mark 11:17.

options.text: He rebuilds Topheth as a place of worship.
options.note: Jesus never rebuilds Topheth; He uses the valley's name, Gehenna, as an image of judgment instead.

options.text: He forbids any future prophet from ever criticizing the temple again.
options.note: Jesus does the opposite, continuing and intensifying this very critique of hollow temple-based religion.

questions: Judah trusted a religious chant, this is the temple of the LORD, as a substitute for a changed life. What correct-sounding religious language or routine might you be leaning on instead of actual obedience?

God warned that His own temple, precious and central as it was, could be destroyed like Shiloh if the lives behind the worship did not change. What in your life have you assumed is untouchable simply because it feels sacred or familiar?
God says obedience, hearing and doing, was always more foundational than ritual sacrifice. Where do you substitute religious activity for actually listening to and obeying what God has said?
Jesus later quoted this very sermon while cleansing the temple of His own generation. How does knowing Jesus takes hollow religion this seriously change how you examine your own worship?

God says the atrocities at Topheth never even entered His mind, exposing how far people can drift while still claiming to serve Him. Where might you need an honest, outside voice to show you how far a practice or belief has drifted from what God actually asked?

translationNotes.note: The threefold repetition, the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD, mimics chant-like liturgical repetition, underscoring that the people treated the phrase almost as an incantation rather than a theological claim requiring a matching life.

The Queen of Heaven likely refers to a Mesopotamian or Canaanite astral deity, possibly Ishtar or Astarte, worshipped by the whole household, showing idolatry had become a normalized family practice rather than an isolated individual sin.

Topheth's name may derive from a word meaning fireplace or hearth, or from a word for shame, deliberately used with contempt for the site of child sacrifice; by the New Testament era this valley's name, Gehenna, had become the standard Jewish term for final judgment.
